summary: Deep technical session focused on embeddings + reranking performance and cost trade-offs. Reviewed vector dimensionality (256 vs 512 vs 1024), batching strategies, KV cache implications for reranking, quantized model options, and VPC/on-prem deployment considerations. Agreed to run baseline benchmarks against a 50k doc corpus with priority on p95 latency and cost per query comparisons between hosted and dedicated deployments.
topics: vector dimensions and accuracy vs cost
KV cache behavior for reranking pipelines
quantization impact on embeddings encoding latency and recall
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We planned 45-60 mins - hope the time works. Quick intros?
[00:08] Alicia Gomez: Hi all, Alicia here. Head of ML at SearchPulse. We're looking into optimizing our rerank pipeline, especially embeddings cost.
[00:15] Tom Rivera: Tom, engineering manager. We're responsible for the infra changes.
[00:20] Sonia Patel: Sonia, platform lead - I'll coordinate the POC networking.
[00:26] Jordan Park: Great. Priya, do you want to kick off with the performance baseline we recommended?
[00:30] Priya Natarajan: Yeah, sure. We usually look at three vector dims: 256, 512, 1024. For reranking specifically, customers often use 512 - good balance of recall vs cost. But we want to test theirs end-to-end because corpus and query distribution matter.
[00:52] Alicia Gomez: We're currently using 512 in prod for retrieval, then a BERT-style cross-encoder for final rerank - which is expensive. We're exploring dense rerankers to replace the cross-encoder.
[01:05] Priya Natarajan: Makes sense. So two parts: embedding encode cost/latency and rerank cost. For embeddings, batching helps throughput but hurts tail latency. What are your p95 targets?
[01:18] Alicia Gomez: Target p95 for the whole flow (retrieve + rerank) is 250 ms. Ideally <200ms, but that's aggressive for 50 qps.
[01:28] Jordan Park: Important for sizing - 50 qps with 250ms p95 is medium-high. For hosted vs dedicated, the big lever is batch sizing and whether you can accept slightly higher p99.
[01:40] Tom Rivera: On infra, we prefer dedicated for isolation but will consider hosted if cost-effective. Also we need VPC + customer KMS.
[01:48] Liam Chen: We support both. On Dedicated, you get reserved capacity which helps with predictable throughput and better batch packing for cost. For VPC we do private peering and integrate with customer KMS for envelope encryption.
[02:03] Sonia Patel: For on-prem POC, is there an air-gapped option? We have a compliance window to check.
[02:09] Jordan Park: Yes, Private/on-prem packages exist - requires more setup (images, keys, and network) but doable. We'll share the checklist.
[02:18] Priya Natarajan: Back to perf: another big factor is rerank top-K. If you rerank top-10 vs top-50 it changes costs drastically. What K are you currently using?
[02:27] Alicia Gomez: We pull top-100 from ANN and currently run cross-encoder on top-20. Thinking of reducing to top-50 and using a lightweight reranker.
[02:36] Priya Natarajan: Good candidate. Embedding dims: 512 will have roughly double compute & memory vs 256, and 1024 is another 2x. But recall improvements diminish after a point. We'll benchmark 256/512.
[02:50] Tom Rivera: For batching, what sizes are reasonable? We worry about latency spike if batch waits for full batch.
[02:58] Priya Natarajan: Typical approach: dynamic batching with max batch size 64 or 128 and a max wait of 10-20ms. For embeddings encode, batch size 64 often yields 3-5x throughput improvement on GPU. But that introduces scheduling delay; you tune based on SLO.
[03:15] Jordan Park: Also consider continuous batching and prefix caching: if many queries share prefixes, KV cache reduces autoregressive workloads - less relevant for straight embedding encoding but crucial if you do decoder-style rerankers.
[03:29] Alicia Gomez: Our reranker is bi-encoder candidate scoring right now, so KV cache isn't huge for that piece. But if we move to generative reranking or cross-encoder, KV/cache matters.
[03:40] Priya Natarajan: Exactly. For cross-encoders the KV cache for sequence models and KV reuse reduces repeated work if reranker is autoregressive or decoder-based. If you only use bi-encoder dot-prod, then batching and optimized BLAS on CPU or GPU is the main thing.
[03:56] Tom Rivera: On cost, can you share typical per-query cost for 512-d and 256-d? ballpark.
[04:03] Liam Chen: Ballpark for hosted embeddings encode on GPU we see cost differences: 512-d might be ~1.8-2x of 256-d per token/encode depending on kernel. But key driver is throughput and reserved vs burst. With Dedicated the per-query cost drops 20-40% at scale due to better packing.
[04:22] Alicia Gomez: When you say 20-40% at scale, what scale specifically?
[04:28] Jordan Park: Usually at sustained workloads >100 qps. For 50 qps we might see smaller delta, but still benefits if you reserve capacity.
[04:35] Priya Natarajan: Also consider quantization. For embedding models we can quantize weights (INT8/4-bit) - that reduces memory and sometimes increases inference throughput, but can slightly degrade vector quality. We should A/B 8-bit vs FP16 for your recall metric.
[04:51] Alicia Gomez: How big is the recall hit typically? For our use case small recall drops degrade UX.
[04:57] Priya Natarajan: Usually 0-2% recall drop for many models at 8-bit; 4-bit is riskier but sometimes acceptable. Depends on model family and dataset. We'll check with your eval set.
[05:08] Tom Rivera: For rerank compute, would you recommend CPU or GPU? Our current infra prefers CPU for cost reasons.
[05:16] Priya Natarajan: For dot-product scoring of bi-encoders, high concurrency on CPU with AVX and BLAS can be fine for moderate QPS. For heavy throughput and larger dims (>768) GPUs start to win. Also for cross-encoders/generative rerankers you typically need GPU.
[05:32] Jordan Park: The general pattern: use CPU for retrieval and scoring at low QPS with small dims; move to GPU when you want lower latency at high QPS or you're using models that require GPU ops.
[05:44] Alicia Gomez: Our current bill is spiky. Would Dedicated smooth costs?
[05:49] Liam Chen: Dedicated provides predictable commit pricing and generally lower unit cost for continuous workloads. You can also configure burst capacity for occasional spikes.
[06:00] Tom Rivera: Can Redwood run a benchmark using our sample dataset (50k docs) and simulate 50 qps with our query distribution?
[06:06] Priya Natarajan: Yes, we can. We'll run encode-only and full rerank flows, test dims 256/512, batch sizes 16/64/256, top-10 vs top-50 rerank. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 latency and cost-per-query.
[06:20] Jordan Park: We'll also include quantized runs (8-bit) to measure recall and latency.
[06:26] Alicia Gomez: Great. For the rerank we want to keep p95 under 250ms. If you can't get there with top-50, we'll consider hybrid approach.
[06:35] Priya Natarajan: Hybrid is common: coarse retrieval with embeddings, then a fast lightweight reranker, only fall back to cross-encoder for a small percent of queries or flagged cases.
[06:45] Tom Rivera: Network-wise for VPC, what are the latency expectations for peered Dedicated vs on-prem?
[06:51] Liam Chen: Peered Dedicated in same cloud region is low single-digit ms between your app and Redwood nodes. On-prem will depend on network hop and VPN - can add 10-30ms if there's a long route. That's important for p95.
[07:06] Sonia Patel: For KMS, do you support customer-managed keys and HSM?
[07:10] Jordan Park: Yes. We support CMKs via major cloud KMS providers and can integrate with HSM for Private deployments. We'll share KMS integration doc.
[07:19] Alicia Gomez: Anything specific to watch for with quantization on retrieval vector norms? We normalize before indexing.
[07:25] Priya Natarajan: Normalize as you do; quantization can change numeric distribution slightly. We'll verify top-k recall after quantization and adjust thresholding if needed. Also the ANN index (HNSW/IVF) parameters interact with vector dims - higher dims often require more ef/search params for equivalent recall, which impacts lookup latency.
[07:45] Tom Rivera: So tuning indexes will be part of the benchmark too.
[07:48] Priya Natarajan: Yes. We'll include index tuning: ef/search, M, and sharding factors.
[07:55] Jordan Park: Let's talk about instrumentation: we'll collect per-route token counts, per-request timing (encode, ANN search, rerank) - that'll help allocate cost.
[08:04] Alicia Gomez: We need that detail for billing owners.
[08:07] Priya Natarajan: We'll produce a spreadsheet with p50/p95/p99, qps, cost per 1k queries, and recall metrics.
[08:15] Tom Rivera: On SLA and monitoring, can Redwood surface p95 per-route in the console?
[08:21] Liam Chen: Yes, per-route dashboards and per-model latency and cost breakdowns are available. You can set alerts for regressions.
[08:29] Alicia Gomez: Any gotchas with batch size 256? I've heard it sometimes increases tail latency dramatically if traffic is low.
[08:36] Priya Natarajan: Right - very large static batch sizes can increase queuing. We prefer dynamic batching with a timeout. For low qps, small batch sizes with GPU warmup avoidance works better. For high qps sustained, larger batches are efficient.
[08:50] Jordan Park: Also consider micro-batching at the application layer combined with Redwood's batching - sending small bursts when you need lower latency per user.
[08:59] Tom Rivera: For the POC, what's required from our side? Data, query samples?
[09:03] Priya Natarajan: Sample corpus (50k docs) as JSONL or parquet, sample query traces with timestamps and expected ground truth for recall eval, and a representative traffic histogram. Also access method details for VPC or temporary S3 for hosted trial.
[09:18] Alicia Gomez: We'll prepare those and share by next week.
[09:22] Sonia Patel: About cross-talk: sorry, my connection is laggy - can you repeat the quantization part?
[09:26] Priya Natarajan: Sure - we'll test 8-bit quantization for the encoder. Often we see improved throughput and lower memory; recall drop typically small, but need to validate on your eval set. We'll also do FP16 baseline.
[09:40] Jordan Park: Anything else on architecture changes you foresee?
[09:44] Alicia Gomez: We might need a small feature store for precomputed embeddings for low-latency updates. How does Redwood handle precomputed vectors?
[09:53] Liam Chen: We can ingest precomputed vectors; just need consistent normalization and schema. For updates we recommend batch ingestion and shard planning to smooth indexing.
[10:05] Priya Natarajan: For realtime updates, you can do hybrid: precompute for the bulk and incremental for hot docs.
[10:13] Tom Rivera: Is there support for reranking caching? If same query appears often, can you cache rerank results?
[10:19] Priya Natarajan: Yes - result caching at route-level is supported. Also query fingerprinting helps. But for personalized queries it's less effective.
[10:30] Alicia Gomez: Regarding evaluation metrics, we'll provide MAP and nDCG. Will you accept those as-is?
[10:34] Priya Natarajan: Absolutely - we'll compute both and present comparisons across dims/quantization/settings.
[10:40] Jordan Park: Quick note - we'll try to keep benchmark runs reproducible and include seed/config.
[10:46] Sonia Patel: One last on security: we need audit logs retention for 12 months. Is that available?
[10:53] Liam Chen: Audit logs and long-term retention are part of our enterprise add-on. We'll include retention SLAs in the doc.
[10:59] Alicia Gomez: Great. Happy with the plan.
[11:02] Jordan Park: To recap: Redwood to run benchmarks (Priya), Jordan to send pricing/security, customer to share dataset & SLOs. We'll reconvene after results.
[11:12] Tom Rivera: Sounds good. Thanks all.
[53:45] meeting end: call ended after ~54 minutes
